questions.q: Given const obj = { a: 1 }, what does obj.b evaluate to?
options: undefined — accessing a missing property doesn't throw an error
It throws a ReferenceError
null
questions.explain: JavaScript object property access is forgiving — a missing property simply evaluates to undefined.

questions.q: Which three places does this lesson say JavaScript shows up in a real dApp?
options: The frontend, the libraries that talk to the chain, and backend/scripts
Only inside the smart contract itself
Only in the wallet extension, nowhere else
Only on blockchain explorer websites
questions.explain: Frontend UI, chain-communication libraries like ethers.js/viem, and Node.js backend/scripts are the three places named.

questions.q: Why is console.table specifically useful for blockchain-related debugging?
options: It renders an array of objects as an actual table, which matches the shape most blockchain data (lists of transactions, balances) comes in
It is the only console method that works with numbers
It automatically connects to a blockchain node
It replaces the need for console.log entirely
questions.explain: Arrays of objects are exactly the shape of most blockchain data, and console.table renders that shape far more readably than nested braces.

questions.q: In const { gasPrice = 0n } = transaction;, when does gasPrice get the value 0n?
options: Only when transaction.gasPrice is missing or undefined
Every single time, regardless of what transaction.gasPrice actually holds
Never — defaults aren't supported in object destructuring
Only if transaction itself is undefined
questions.explain: A destructuring default applies specifically when the property is missing or explicitly undefined.

questions.q: What does const status = balance > 0 ? "funded" : "empty"; do?
options: It's a ternary expression: a compact if/else that assigns "funded" if balance > 0 is true, otherwise "empty"
It always assigns "funded" regardless of balance
It throws a syntax error because ternary expressions don't exist in JavaScript
It assigns both "funded" and "empty" at once
questions.explain: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse evaluates the condition once and assigns exactly one of the two values.

questions.q: What does .map() return, and what happens to the original array?
options: A new array of the same length with every element transformed; the original array is never changed
The same array, modified in place
A single combined value, not an array
A shorter array containing only elements that passed a test
questions.explain: map() produces a brand-new array of transformed values and leaves the original array untouched.

questions.q: What is the call stack?
options: A browser extension for debugging
A queue of HTTP requests waiting to be sent
Where JavaScript's synchronous code actually executes, one function frame at a time
A list of all variables currently in scope
questions.explain: The call stack tracks which function is currently running; JavaScript only runs one thing on it at a time.

questions.q: What is the benefit of wrapping fetch, response.ok checking, and JSON parsing inside one function like getEthPrice?
options: It makes the API respond faster
Calling code doesn't need to know about fetch, Response objects, or rejections — it just awaits a value or checks for null
It removes the need for async/await entirely
It bypasses CORS restrictions
questions.explain: Encapsulating the complexity once means every caller gets a simple, predictable interface instead of repeating fetch/parsing/error-handling logic everywhere.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three problems associated with deeply nested callbacks discussed in this lesson?
options: Increasing rightward indentation with each nested step
Error handling repeated at every level
Difficulty reusing a step locked inside another callback
Callbacks running in a random, non-deterministic order
questions.explain: Callback order isn't random — it follows the event loop's rules covered in the previous lesson. The real pain points are nesting depth, repeated error handling, and poor reusability.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue TypeScript matters especially in blockchain development?
options: Because blockchain code can't run without it
Because real funds are on the line and smart contract ABIs have many typed parameters, so catching a type mismatch before deployment matters a lot
Because Solidity requires TypeScript
Because TypeScript makes transactions execute faster on-chain
questions.explain: A wrong-type bug in code that moves real funds, or that calls a contract with many ABI-typed parameters, is far costlier to discover after deployment than before it.

questions.q: What does function pair<K, V>(key: K, value: V): [K, V] demonstrate that first<T> does not?
options: That generics can only be used with arrays
That a generic function can declare more than one independent type parameter
That generics are unrelated to type inference
That TypeScript doesn't support tuples
questions.explain: pair has two type parameters, K and V, each inferred independently from its own argument — showing generics aren't limited to a single placeholder.

questions.q: What's the difference between number[] and a tuple like [string, number]?
options: There is no difference
number[] allows any number of elements of that type; a tuple fixes both the exact length and the type at each position
Tuples can only hold numbers
number[] is stricter than a tuple
questions.explain: An array type like number[] can be any length, all the same type; a tuple locks in a specific length with a specific type per position.

questions.q: Why does setting module/moduleResolution to "NodeNext" matter for a web3 project specifically?
options: NodeNext makes bigint literals compile on older targets
NodeNext disables strict mode automatically
Many web3 libraries ship ESM-only, and NodeNext resolves imports the way modern Node.js actually handles a package's "type" field and exports map
NodeNext is required to use JSON imports
questions.explain: Older CommonJS-style module resolution can silently break on ESM-only packages with a confusing "cannot find module" error; NodeNext resolves imports the way Node.js itself does.

questions.q: Why might a project prefer a Result<T> return type over simply throwing an exception on a failed contract read?
options: Because exceptions are not supported in TypeScript
Because Result<T> runs the contract call twice for safety
Because throwing is slower than returning an object
Because it's easy for a caller to forget a try/catch, while Result<T> makes the failure case part of the type signature the compiler enforces
questions.explain: Exceptions are easy to forget to handle; encoding success/failure directly in the return type means the compiler can require the caller to check `result.ok` before accessing `value`.

questions.q: In the lesson's Transaction interface, why is `to: Address | null` instead of just `to: Address`?
options: Because TypeScript requires every field to be nullable
Because Address can never be assigned directly
Because a contract-creation transaction has no destination address
Because null makes the interface compile faster
questions.explain: A contract-creation transaction genuinely has no `to` address, so modeling it as nullable forces code to handle that real case instead of assuming every transaction has a destination.

questions.q: What does `process.exit(1)` signal to anything running or chaining this script (a shell, CI pipeline, or cron job)?
options: That the script succeeded
That the script failed — any nonzero exit code signals "something went wrong" to automated tooling
That the script is still running
It has no effect outside of a human reading console output
questions.explain: Automated tooling (CI, cron, shell && chains) decides what to do next based on the exit code, not printed output — 0 means success, any nonzero code signals failure.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies` in package.json?
options: dependencies are needed for the program to run (e.g. ethers); devDependencies are only needed while building/developing (e.g. the TypeScript compiler), and can be skipped in production with --omit=dev
There is no real difference — npm treats them identically
devDependencies are always installed globally, dependencies are always local
dependencies can only be npm's own built-in packages
questions.explain: dependencies ship with the running program; devDependencies (like typescript or tsx) are only needed to build or develop it, and a production install can skip them with --omit=dev.

questions.q: What does `readFile(path, "utf-8")` return, compared to calling `readFile(path)` with no encoding argument?
options: It returns a plain string instead of a raw Buffer of bytes
It returns a Promise that never resolves
It deletes the file after reading
It returns the file size in bytes only
questions.explain: Without an encoding, readFile resolves with a Buffer (raw bytes); passing "utf-8" decodes it into a plain string, which is what you want for JSON or text files.

questions.q: Why does getChainSnapshot use Promise.all for the blockNumber and balance reads instead of awaiting them one after another?
options: Because Promise.all is required syntax for any async function
Because the two reads don't depend on each other's result, so running them concurrently is strictly faster than awaiting them sequentially
Because ethers does not allow sequential awaits
Because Promise.all automatically retries failed calls
questions.explain: getBlockNumber and getBalance are independent reads; Promise.all lets both RPC calls happen concurrently rather than waiting for one to finish before starting the other.

questions.q: What is described as the capstone's optional stretch goal, not required for a complete capstone?
options: Writing a smart contract in Solidity
Wrapping chain.ts's logic in the Lesson 36 Express server to expose GET /balance/:address as a real HTTP endpoint
Deploying to a Kubernetes cluster
Rewriting the project in Python
questions.explain: The lesson names the Express wrapper from Lesson 36, exposing the balance lookup as an HTTP endpoint, as an optional extension beyond the CLI tool that's actually required.

questions.q: Which chapter does this lesson credit with applying TypeScript specifically to blockchain data and real libraries like ethers/viem?
options: Chapter 4 (TypeScript Fundamentals)
Chapter 6 (Node.js Basics)
Chapter 5 (TypeScript for Blockchain Development)
Chapter 1 (Programming Fundamentals Through JavaScript)
questions.explain: The course recap explicitly assigns Chapter 5 to applying TypeScript to blockchain data, ethers/viem, type-safe contract calls, project configuration, and recurring patterns.
